There was a fellow named Earl who drove all the way down from Rocky Mount to Rodanthe just to catch a trophy red drum in the Outer Banks surf. He brought a twelve-foot rod that cost more than his first truck, and he spent fifty dollars on fresh mullet down at the tackle shop.

Every ten minutes he’d holler back to his buddy Clayton that he could feel the nibbles starting, while Clayton just sat on a five-gallon bucket in the dry sand, holding a cheap cane pole with a piece of shrimp dangling in a shallow tidal pool barely six inches deep.

For three hours Earl fought the ghost fish, sweating through his flannel shirt and cussing the bluefish for stealing his bait, while Clayton dozed in the sun. Then suddenly, Earl’s reel started screaming like a scalded cat, line flying off the spool so fast it nearly smoked. He dug his heels in, backed up onto the dunes, and hollered for a net as he fought that brute through the heavy surf.

Just as Earl dragged a massive, thrashing thirty-pound red drum gasping into the shallow foam, Clayton reached down lazily beside his left boot, scooped his bare hand into that mud puddle, and hoisted out a thirty-five-pound black drum that looked like a manhole cover. Earl stared at his prize catch, looked down at Clayton’s puddle, and didn't touch another fishing rod the rest of the week.

There was a fellow down in Sampson County named Cecil Oates who prided himself on never backing down from an inch of dirt. When his neighbor, old man Culbreth, planted a black walnut tree so close to the property line that the roots were practically drinking out of Cecil’s well, Cecil didn’t complain. He just waited until October, swept every single walnut that fell on his side into five-gallon buckets, and dumped them right back in Culbreth’s driveway before sunrise.

Culbreth didn't say a word about the buckets. Instead, he rented a three-piece brass band from Wilmington, set them up on his porch at dawn on a Saturday, and had them play solemn funeral marches every time Cecil walked out to get his morning paper. Cecil countered by buying an antique foghorn off a fishing boat in Engelhard and mounting it to his porch post, tuned to go off whenever the wind blew out of the east.

For three weeks, the neighborhood sounded like a foggy harbor where somebody had died of melancholy. The sheriff finally came out, drank a glass of iced tea on Cecil's porch, and pointed out after a spell of looking at the deeds that the walnut tree wasn't Culbreth's at all, but sat entirely on the county right-of-way.

Neither man blinked. The very next morning, Cecil and Culbreth were out there together with crosscut saws, cutting the tree down to a stump just so neither one of them had to look at another nut. By noon, they were sitting on upside-down peach baskets sharing a jar of blackberry cider, cussing out the county commissioners for planting the doggone thing in the first place.
